Macro strength is a V2 coincident heuristic (Fed Funds 21d/126d panic-cut; 10y-2y level and 21d/126d un-inversion; UNRATE Sahm proxy), not a probability or forecast.

S&P 500 levels are daily S&P composite closes from Yahoo Finance (^GSPC) from 1927-12-30. Official S&P 500 closes (S&P Dow Jones Indices, via FRED) replace Yahoo's on 9 dates where Yahoo's close was off by more than half a cent; isolated Yahoo misprints on 6 dates (1935-1961) are dropped, so the previous close carries forward. The artifact metadata lists every such date. Before 1957-03-04 the index is the S&P 90, the S&P 500's predecessor, and pre-1952 Saturday sessions are absent. Before 1927-12-30 the series is the NBER/Cowles monthly stock index (1935-39=100), forward-filled to daily. The two segments are not chained, so levels compare only within a segment; prices exclude dividends.

The S&P 1-year volatility, drawdown and volatility-percentile windows restart where the daily series begins (1927-12-30), so volatility is empty until 1928-05-03, drawdown until 1928-05-02 and the volatility percentile until 1929-01-09. Yahoo's daily history has 8 runs of three or more identical consecutive closes; the longest is 4 sessions at 11.48 (1943-04-22 to 1943-04-28) and the latest 3 sessions at 109.02 (1979-08-28 to 1979-08-30). Some may be stale vendor prints; with no independent daily source to check them, they are kept as delivered and listed in the artifact metadata.
USREC is excluded from the strength inputs to avoid target leakage.

Gold is the World Bank Pink Sheet London bullion benchmark forward-filled to daily; bonds are a 7.5-duration 10y UST total-return proxy; the dollar target is the broad trade-weighted index; Bitcoin is the Blockchain.com daily market price from 2010-08-18.
Nifty 50 daily prices come from Yahoo Finance (^NSEI). Yahoo's history begins in 2007, so the Nifty series is intentionally unavailable before then.

Core Index v2 is a weekly trend-and-stress state machine on the daily S&P 500 (the S&P 90 before March 1957), with credit spreads, unemployment and the yield curve as stress inputs, each lagged by its publication delay. It is decided at each Friday close and held until the next; it starts at the end of 1928, once a year of daily closes exists. Until 1948 only the Baa-Aaa credit spread and volatility can raise stress flags; unemployment joins in 1949 and the yield curve in 1953. The four bands keep their allocation meaning; severity describes the decline under way. Not a forecast.

FRED's keyless CSV endpoint exposes only a rolling three-year ICE BofA HY OAS window. The pipeline merges FRED's recent observations with a cached public 1996+ mirror; the official FRED API path retains the full provider history.
Crypto milestone dates are editorial comparison windows, not statistically detected events or NBER recession dates.
